tagline: Along the North Platte, wagon traffic left its marks in stone
intro: The Oregon Trail Historic Byway follows U.S. 26 west from the Nebraska border to Dwyer Junction, connecting Torrington, Lingle, Fort Laramie and Guernsey. Between Torrington and Guernsey, the drive follows the North Platte River corridor. Wyoming’s tourism office gives this historic byway a length of 57 miles and advises an hour and a half without stops. It highlights the surviving fort structures, emigrant inscriptions and wagon ruts cut into rock. Register Cliff rises a hundred feet above the valley floor, with emigrants’ inscriptions still visible.

The older trail carried traders, trappers and missionaries before the wagon migrations of the 1840s. Near Guernsey, the route avoided marshy river ground by crossing a sandstone ridge. Wheels, animals and people wore down that rock during heavy use from 1841 to 1869. Completion of the Union Pacific Railroad in 1869 sharply reduced overland trail travel, though local use continued.

Begin at the Nebraska line, near the marker for the Oregon Trail’s entry into Wyoming. Torrington’s former Union Pacific depot houses the Homesteaders Museum. Continue through Lingle to the town of Fort Laramie; the historic post lies south across the North Platte. Near Guernsey, a short trail reaches the wagon ruts before the byway ends at Interstate 25.

moments.title: Torrington
moments.text: Torrington’s Homesteaders Museum occupies a preserved Union Pacific depot, a railway building in a town that began as a railroad service point. The early watering and coaling station belonged to the CB&Q Railroad, which began passenger service here in 1900. Farmers and ranchers gathered in the new town. The town became a trading center for Goshen County and nearby parts of Wyoming and Nebraska. Union Pacific came later, constructing a spur from Cheyenne to South Torrington in 1925 to serve a proposed sugar plant. The museum’s setting brings that later railway chapter into the story of the surrounding agricultural community.

moments.title: Fort Laramie
moments.text: Fort Laramie began as a private fur-trading post; the U.S. Army bought it in 1849. The fort stood east of the long climb toward South Pass, an important Rocky Mountain crossing for wagon travelers. It became a stop for emigrant wagon trains and a military post during the Plains Indian Wars. Old Bedlam, built in 1849, housed officers who shared rooms and communal kitchens. The Army abandoned the fort in 1890. The surviving complex includes standing buildings and ruins, preserved by the National Park Service. These are remnants of a larger post: the remaining structures represent only a third of the buildings once here.

moments.title: Oregon Trail Ruts
moments.text: The wagons took the ridge to avoid marshy ground beside the North Platte River. That choice concentrated traffic on sandstone: wagon wheels, draft animals and people wore the trail into the rock during heavy use from 1841 to 1869. Even after railroad completion reduced westbound trail traffic in 1869, portions remained in local use for years. The preserved stretch is half a mile long, with ruts two to six feet deep. It lies south of both Guernsey and the river. A short walking trail leads to the deep gouges cut into the rock by wagon wheels.
